title: They are still. Once quick in the brains of men. Still: but an itch of death is in them, to tell me in my ear a maudlin tale, urge me to wreak their will.
html_source:
As Stephen asked St. Ignatius of Loyola for help earlier in this episode, he needs help again but seeks it from a very different source. His thoughts and words are far more loaded in this stream of consciousness.

http://lit.genius.com/3368906

Interpreting the words literally makes one concerned about his mental stability.Our retrospect throws heard the voice, moonycrowned, itch of death, painted chambers quickly into the bag of madness however they are thoughtallusions grounded in whatever substratum the rest of his psyche lies.

With Stephen steering between the Scylla rock logic of Aristotle and the Charybdis mystical whirlpool of Plato, many critics see the resultant force veer into Freud and psychoanalysis in this paragraph. (A Concise Companion to Psychoanalysis, Literature, and Culture,edited by Laura Marcus, Ankhi Mukherjee).

He steers a median between logic and universals with ‘embalmed in spice of words’. The art of the author does live on through their book coffins but that’s it, there is no access to mystical-beyond-us truths, they are human not formal logic.

anchor.prefix: ses, embalmed in spice of words. Thoth, god of libraries, a birdgod, moonycrowned. And I heard the voice of that Egyptian highpriest. In painted chambers loaded with tilebooks.
anchor.suffix: — Certainly, John Eglinton mused, of all great men he is the most enigmatic. We know nothing but that he lived and suffered. Not even so much. Others abide our question. A shad
